# Finish textures

What the 3D page puts on cabinet fronts, worktops and the floor, so the
quick pictures and the renders look like real materials. The Studio's 3D view
(`frontend/`) builds these same files into its bundle: after replacing one,
run `npm run build` in `frontend/` as well.

**These are stand-ins.** They were generated by `tool/gen_finish_textures.py`
(original, procedural; no photographs and no licensed images). They read as
oak, walnut, birch, quartz, marble, granite, slate, terrazzo and a plank
floor, but they are not SS Love's actual finishes. When the designer sends
photographs of the real samples, they replace these files; nothing else needs
to change.

## What is here

`manifest.json` lists every texture: its files, its real-world size and its
kind. Each texture is up to three images:

| File | What | Format |
|---|---|---|
| `<id>_albedo.jpg` | the colour | 1024×1024 (floor: 2048×2048), sRGB, tiles seamlessly |
| `<id>_normal.jpg` | the relief (grain, pores, cleft) | 512×512, tangent-space normal map, +Y up |
| `<id>_rough.jpg` | how shiny each part is (dark = shiny) | 512×512, greyscale |

Only the albedo is required. Polished stone has no normal map. `micro_*.jpg`
is the faint orange-peel of a matte painted or laminate front, used with a
flat colour.

| id | Used for |
|---|---|
| `oak_light` | Japandi base and tall units |
| `birch` | Nordic tall units |
| `walnut` | Industrial base and tall units |
| `quartz_warm` | Japandi worktop |
| `quartz_snow` | Minimalist worktop |
| `terrazzo` | Nordic worktop |
| `slate_dark` | Industrial worktop |
| `calacatta`, `granite_black` | the benchtop choices *Calacatta Engineered Quartz* and *Nero Absolute Granite* |
| `tile_subway`, `tile_hex` | the backsplash: 150×75 mm subway bricks and a hexagon mosaic (0.6 m per tile; the hexagon sheet is not square, `tile_h_m` in the manifest says how tall) |
| `floor_oak` | the room's floor (about 2.4 m of plank floor per tile) |

Painted fronts (the white wall units, Minimalist's charcoal, Nordic's sage)
are a flat colour plus the micro texture, not a photograph.

## Swapping in real photographs

1. Photograph or scan the sample flat and square-on, in even light, then make
   it tile seamlessly (any image editor's offset-and-heal, or a texture tool).
2. Crop it to cover `tile_m` metres (0.8 m for wood, 1.2 m for stone; the
   floor 2.4 m). Wood grain must run **top to bottom**: doors are mapped with
   the grain along their height.
3. Save as JPEG with the same file name (for example `oak_light_albedo.jpg`),
   1024×1024. Add a `*_normal.jpg` and `*_rough.jpg` if you have them
   (512×512); delete the old ones if you don't.
4. If the real sample covers a different size, change its `tile_m` in
   `manifest.json`. All wood textures share one size, and all stone another
   (the page checks the first of each kind).
5. Keep the whole folder under 4 MB: it is sent to the tablet each time a
   design opens. (A test fails above that.)

A finish that isn't here yet needs a name in the page's `STYLE_FINISHES`
(`tex: '<id>'`) or `BENCHTOP_LOOKS` in `assets/3d/index.html`, and an entry in
`manifest.json`.

## Regenerating the stand-ins

```bash
python tool/gen_finish_textures.py             # rewrites this folder
python tool/gen_finish_textures.py --preview /tmp/tex   # + a contact sheet
```

Needs numpy and Pillow. It is deterministic. It overwrites any photographs
you have put here, so don't run it afterwards.
